title: Text, Filters, and Now Vectors in One Postgres Index
summary: We added vectors to the ParadeDB index and tested filtered queries against Turbopuffer and other Postgres vector extensions.
body_markdown:
# Text, Filters, and Now Vectors in One Postgres Index


By Ming Ying, Ruchir Raj, and Walter Woodall on November 19, 2026


A visualization of theParadeDB cluster-based index


The explosion in` pgvector` use has shown how valuable vectors are alongside the relational data they represent. But once you move past toy examples and benchmarks, most heavy users of Postgres vector indexes will struggle to scale in production because they trip up on:


- **Filtering** : Complex` WHERE` clauses can slow queries dramatically or reduce recall.
- **Memory** : Large datasets demand more memory to build and search.
- **Continuous updates** : Heavy writes add maintenance work to preserve recall and performance.


Today we're announcing native vector support in ParadeDB. Following in the footsteps of search engines, vectors live in the same index that powers text search, addressing filtering and memory together. Support for continuous updates is still in development.


Rather than compare against just Postgres vector extensions, we decided to raise the bar and benchmark against a dedicated search engine. Here's how we compare with Turbopuffer on vector search over the 28 million-row Hacker News dataset1 , with a 0.01% selectivity text filter:

In the following sections, we'll first share some more performance results. Then, we'll do a deep dive into our architecture and roadmap.


## Why We Benchmarked Against Turbopuffer


To keep search in Postgres, we need to be competitive with dedicated search engines. Being faster than another Postgres vector index matters less if an external vector database performs significantly better. We benchmark against Turbopuffer, which we consider to be one of the most popular vector databases, to test that.


ParadeDB excels at both unfiltered and filtered vector search. For unfiltered search we use the 113 million MS Marco dataset. Here ParadeDB delivers 1.7× Turbopuffer's throughput for top-10 search, at 95.2% versus 94% measured recall2 .


Interactive benchmark chart


Before we continue, we'd like to note that an apples-to-apples comparison was not fully possible for a few reasons:


1. **Different Recalls** : ParadeDB exposes a query-time knob to tune recall3 , but Turbopuffer does not. Queries are faster at lower recall, so comparisons of different vector engines should be done at equal recall. For most of these comparisons, the recalls of ParadeDB and Turbopuffer differ slightly and are shown in the graphs.
2. **Different Hardware** : Postgres benchmarks were run on AWS EC2` c8gd.metal-24xl` instances with local NVMe SSD storage, with each database running in a Docker container limited to 8 CPUs and 32 GiB of RAM4 . Aside from its use of[NVMe SSDs for caching](https://turbopuffer.com/docs/architecture) , Turbopuffer's exact hardware configuration and the CPU and memory resources allocated are unknown to us.
3. **Network Latency** : Because Turbopuffer runs on their cloud (we do not have access to their BYOC), they are disadvantaged in our benchmarks by sub-1ms network latency.


For these reasons we are not claiming to be faster than Turbopuffer, even if it appears that way in the results. Instead, we are including Turbopuffer to demonstrate that you can expect comparable vector search performance between the two databases, running ParadeDB on a modest 8 CPUs and 32GB RAM. This is not the case for any other Postgres vector extension. As you will see below, in some filtered cases they are hundreds of times slower and miss ranges of recall targets.


Our results are reproducible with[benchmarker](https://github.com/paradedb/benchmarker) and we welcome verification.


## What Happens When We Add Filters?


On the 28M Hacker News dataset, we tested top-10 searches with date range and text filters. For instance, a ParadeDB vector search with a date range filter looks like:


```text
SELECT   id  FROM   hn_items
WHERE   id @@@ pdb.all()
AND    time    >=    '2021-09-09T06:23:25+00:00'  ::timestamptz
ORDER    BY   emb  <=>    '[...]'  ::vector( 1536  )
LIMIT  10  ;


```


A text filter looks like:


```text
SELECT   id  FROM   hn_items
WHERE   id @@@ pdb.all()
AND   "by"  =    'rossdavidh'
ORDER    BY   emb  <=>    '[...]'  ::vector( 1536  )
LIMIT  10  ;


```


In our benchmarks, ParadeDB is competitive with Turbopuffer at lower selectivities and races ahead at higher selectivities. For instance, with text filters matching 0.01% and 0.001% of the dataset, ParadeDB delivers 3.9× and 5.6× Turbopuffer's throughput, respectively, at 100% measured recall.


Interactive benchmark chart


## How We Built It: A Filter-Aware Index


The ParadeDB index was already[filter-aware](https://www.paradedb.com/docs/reference/filtering/overview) for text search and facets.


The tricky part about extending that ability to vectors is that more selective filters require deeper, more expensive probing into the vector index where large amounts of work could get thrown away. With` pgvector` and every other vector extension,[filters are applied after vector candidates are found](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector#filtering) . This means that, under a 1% selectivity filter, only 1 out of 100 vectors read and scored could actually make it into the result set. The rest is wasted work.


ParadeDB avoids that wasted work because vectors and filterable fields share an index. For the Hacker News queries above, vectors are indexed alongside the fields that support text search and range filtering:


```text
CREATE   INDEX hn_search_idx  ON   hn_items
USING   paradedb (
id,
title,
("by"::pdb.literal),
time  ,
emb vector_cosine_ops
);


```


Before doing any vector-related work, ParadeDB first evaluates the filter(s) into a bitset of matching document identifiers. During vector search, the index checks each candidate's identifier against the bitset before it loads or scores the vector. Candidates that fail the filter incur only a fast bitset check instead of an expensive vector calculation.


To see just how efficient ParadeDB is at evaluating filters, the following graph compares throughput over the Cohere 10M dataset at three different selectivities: 1%, 10%, and unfiltered. Notice how, for a given recall target, the filtered queries are similarly as fast as the unfiltered queries.


Interactive benchmark chart


This is not the case with any other Postgres extension because of a fundamental architectural difference: they require separate indexes for vectors and other fields. We discussed in a[previous blog post](https://www.paradedb.com/blog/opening-a-closed-tin-part-2#now-for-the-rest-of-search) how performance-critical it is for filters to be indexed alongside text. The same is true for vectors.


Here is the same filtered-versus-unfiltered comparison for` vectorchord` and` pg_vectorsearch` . At the 95% recall target, applying a 1% filter reduces` vectorchord` 's throughput by 70× and` pg_vectorsearch` 's by an estimated 92×.


Interactive benchmark chart

Additionally, we tested six filters matching from 10% down to 0.001% of rows at three recall targets. Only ParadeDB reached all 18 recall targets.` vectorchord` reached 16, while` pg_vectorsearch` reached three.


Generally speaking, the more selective the filters become, the worse the other Postgres extensions perform. For example,` pg_vectorsearch` 's highest achieved recall on the 0.001% text filter was 16.4%, at near-zero estimated throughput.


Interactive benchmark chart


Unfiltered vector search is a closer contest, and is where the existing Postgres vector extensions do well. On the MS MARCO 113 million dataset4 :


- ParadeDB delivers 2.0×–9.5× the throughput of` vectorchord` across the board.
- ParadeDB outperforms` pg_vectorsearch` in four of the five comparisons where both reached the recall target.` pg_vectorsearch` leads for top 10 at 90% recall. It missed the top-10 99% recall target.


Interactive benchmark chart


To the best of our knowledge, every other Postgres platform uses one of` pgvector` ,` vectorchord` ,` pg_vectorsearch` , or a rebranded fork for vector search.


## Constraining Memory During Index Build


Vector indexes that require memory usage to increase linearly with dataset size fundamentally do not scale.


For us, the main challenge with constraining memory during index build was making our k-means algorithm bounded in memory. For context, the ParadeDB vector index is acluster-based index , and k-means is the standard algorithm for generating clusters. If not handled carefully, k-means increases memory consumption with dataset size, since larger datasets produce more clusters which require more data points to be sampled.


ParadeDB circumvents this by implementing a streaming k-means algorithm. The idea is that instead of holding the entire training set in memory, we read vectors in batches and do k-means iteration over each batch. We have open-sourced[our k-means implementation](https://github.com/paradedb/superkmeans-rs) . It's a Rust port of[SuperKMeans](https://github.com/cwida/SuperKMeans) , a C++ library developed by researchers at[CWI](https://www.cwi.nl/en/) , with additional features like streaming k-means, cluster balancing, and boundary replication of vectors across clusters.


To demonstrate our memory efficiency, all benchmarks in this post were run on a Docker container with 32GB memory, only 8GB of which was allocated to index build (via` maintenance_work_mem` ). This memory allocation is a tiny fraction of the total dataset and index size. MSMarco's embeddings alone contain approximately 430GB of float values.


Under the 8GB memory constraint, only the ParadeDB index built the MSMarco dataset successfully at its default settings. Both` pg_vectorsearch` and` vectorchord` ran out of memory, crashed, and required adjustments. Because` vectorchord` holds the training set in memory, it requires the k-means sampling rate to be manually dialed down (which degrades the quality of the resulting index).` pg_vectorsearch` had a memory leak that we[fixed](https://github.com/timescale/pg_vectorsearch/pull/417) .


We also optimized our index build time to be very fast. Here's how long it took to index the 113M MSMarco vectors:

## Constraining Memory During Search


One of the reasons we picked a cluster-based vector index over a graph-based index like HNSW is because the access patterns of cluster-based indexes are much more friendly when the index is too big to fit in memory.


Because HNSW follows vector connections scattered throughout a graph, each hop can turn into a random disk read on uncached data. This is why` pgvector` , which uses HNSW, forces many users to raise their instance's memory to the size of the index. It's also why we are skeptical of any HNSW-based vector index's ability to scale.


Cluster-based indexes, on the other hand, store each cluster's vectors contiguously, so searching a cluster translates into sequential reads. Our index is specifically designed to incur as few disk reads as possible. In our benchmarks, we ensure that most of the index cannot simply be cached in memory for search by sizing the Postgres` shared_buffers` pool to` 8GB` .


## A Deeper Look at Our Cluster-Based Architecture


Our architecture draws on the[SPANN](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.08566) and[Quake](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.03437) papers:


1 / 3


### Find the most promising clusters


The starting idea is simple: group similar vectors into clusters, and give each cluster a representative vector called a centroid. A query first finds the nearest centroids, then compares itself against the vectors in just those clusters instead of the entire dataset.


ParadeDB extends this idea into a hierarchy: clusters can be created over clusters. This idea, borrowed from[Quake](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.03437) , allows the centroid list to scale. As the dataset grows, another level in the hierarchy keeps each layer small.


Search starts at the top of the hierarchy and works its way down. Once the bottom is reached, the most promising clusters are visited.


2 / 3


### Scan clusters to eliminate noncompetitive vectors


Each cluster stores quantized vectors. Quantization compresses vectors, allowing noncompetitive vectors to be cheaply eliminated without paying the cost of full precision scoring.


ParadeDB uses a two-layer quantization strategy, where the first layer 1-bit quantizes the vector's residual from its cluster centroid, and the second layer 1-bit quantizes the error left by the first layer. Quantized vectors are also boundary replicated, meaning that a vector sitting close to two clusters is replicated across both. This technique, borrowed from[SPANN](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.08566) , helps with recall.


Filters are also applied here. If a vector's identifier fails the filter, we skip its quantized vector.


3 / 3


### Score the survivors at full precision


Finally, candidates that survive both layers of the quantized scan are ranked by their full precision vectors to produce the final result set. The idea is that each previous pruning step (cluster scan, then two quantized layers) constricts the search space further.


By the time this step is reached, the full precision candidate set is very small (in our 113M MSMarco dataset, only a few hundred candidates survive to this point).


Like the rest of ParadeDB, our vector search implementation is entirely open source:


- [ParadeDB](https://github.com/paradedb/paradedb) : The Postgres extension and SQL integration.


- [Our Tantivy fork](https://github.com/paradedb/tantivy) : Vector indexing, routing, and search. We will upstream as much of this as possible in the coming months.


- [SuperKMeans](https://github.com/paradedb/superkmeans-rs) : Rust port of SuperKMeans for building clusters.


## Continuous Updates are Next


Our next target is support for continuous updates (i.e. preventing frequent updates from affecting recall/performance). We are solving this by allowing clusters to cheaply update themselves as new data arrives. Our approach will lean on both[SPFresh](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.14452) for cluster rebalancing and[segment partitioning](https://www.paradedb.com/docs/reference/indexing/partition-by) to create an optimal distribution of vectors across our segment-based layout.


This means that for now, our vector search is tested and ready for mostly static datasets (i.e. an index that can be created after all the data has been loaded, and new data infrequently arrives). If your vector search workload requires frequently updated data,[contact us](https://www.paradedb.com/contact) . We'd love to work closely with you as we build it.


This is specifically for ParadeDB indexes containing vectors. For all other fields, we[ensure high read performance under continuous writes](https://www.paradedb.com/blog/increased-write-performance) .


## Wrapping Up


ParadeDB already delivers excellent filtered text search to Postgres, eliminating the need for a separate search engine like Elasticsearch. Now we're doing the same for vectors.


Our vector search has already been in beta for two months. The features in this post are available on ParadeDB` 0.27.0` and later. We invite you to run it over your data[locally](https://www.paradedb.com/docs/start/install) or on[ParadeDB Cloud](https://app.paradedb.com/) .
